edits.old: Self-managed and Atlas connection ceilings come from different layers. For self-managed `mongod`, `net.maxIncomingConnections` sets the incoming-connection limit unless a system-wide host limit binds first. Atlas limits vary by cluster tier and class and apply per node; for sharded clusters they apply per `mongos` router. There is no universal maximum-connection number across deployments. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

edits.old: A connection ceiling is not a throughput guarantee: Atlas scales on memory and compute rather than connection count, while increased active connections can add load. (high confidence)

edits.old: MongoDB's `maxPoolSize` caps connections in a single driver pool; it is not a deployment-wide quota. Each `MongoClient` owns its pool or pools, topology-aware drivers create pools for individual servers, and monitoring sockets are additional to application-pool sockets. A connection estimate should sum client instances and destination-server pools, then include monitoring sockets and other clients. (high confidence)
edits.new: MongoDB's `maxPoolSize` caps connections in a single driver pool; it is not a deployment-wide quota. Each `MongoClient` instance manages its own connection pool. Drivers keep a pool per server in the topology (documented for the Go driver), and open additional monitoring sockets per server (two per server in the Go driver docs; drivers open a minimum of 3 connections per node, one application connection plus a monitoring and a round-trip-timing connection, per a MongoDB staff forum answer). A connection estimate should therefore account for the number of client instances and servers, plus monitoring connections. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/administration/connection-pool-overview.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/drivers/go/current/connect/connection-options/connection-pools/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/db-connection-using-mongo-connect-are-by-default-3-in-aws-is-there-a-way-to-set-this-to-1-initially/228830
